newsitem.title: USA: White House sees little support for CPI commission.
newsitem.headline: White House sees little support for CPI commission.

text.p: The White House suggested Thursday that the idea of creating a bipartisan commission to decide changes to the consumer price index (CPI) has been set aside for the moment.

But one administration official said that while there was little support for the idea at present, President Clinton had not made any final decision against it as suggested by a report in the Washington Post Thursday.

Commenting on the report that Clinton had abandoned the idea of an independent panel to reduce the cost-of-living adjustments for federal benefits, White House spokesman Mike McCurry told reporters the idea "has not been warmly received" in Congress.
"There doesn't seem to be enthusiasm for a commission," he said. "That doesn't mean that there aren't other ideas that might work ... That may not be the only way to skin the cat."

Politically, the issue is highly sensitive because Social Security retirement payments and many other federal benefits are linked to the CPI. There appears to be consensus among economists that the CPI overstates inflation but there is little agreement on how to go about addressing the issue.
In part, this is because neither Clinton's Democrats nor the Republicans who control both houses of Congress are eager to bear alone the political cost of trimming the programmes.

A slight reduction in the CPI would have huge consequences for the budget, trimming federal expenditures and providing savings that could be applied to cutting the deficit, offering tax cuts or funding other programmes.
One administration official who asked not to be identified said the president had not ruled out a commission, though the official admitted that it had little support at present.
"Obviously the reception has not been terribly good, but ruled out is really a little excessive," he said.
"Why do they now want us to do it alone? Because they want us to take the heat," he added, saying the only way such changes would be durable was if both parties agreed on them.

"As a matter of simple political reality it will either not happen or even if it happens, (will not) have any steam to remain in place if it's not bipartisan," said the official. "They know it and we know it."
